3525768,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.9.2.7,1985-04-23,c6963b2e-3dd4-4087-b65d-05d62938f08f,ca.m.7212,Mr. Jourdenais:,,PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS,IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND",,"As I was saying: . . . with regard to a refugee program that is very highly esteemed at the international level. However, there is no quick and easy answer to what in recent years has become a very complex immigration problem.

I am sure that all parties concerned . . . Opposition Members want a realistic and humanitarian policy that will help those who are really in need. This means that we must implement a program that makes a distinction between individuals who are likely to abuse the system and those who really need a fair system for the recognition of refugee status.

It is a fact that we are experiencing a number of problems with our system for the recognition of refugees status, even if it is much admired by representatives from the United Nations and other countries. The fact that it has become increasingly difficult to distinguish quickly between bona fide refugees and individuals who are only trying to take advantage of the system for personal reasons has become a very big and complex problem. We must find answers that are not too simplistic, that will not aggravate the present situation and will not make the difficult task of helping bona fide refugees even more difficult.

The Convention of Geneva on the Status of Refugees defines a refugee as a person who, owing to well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of his nationality and is unable or, owing
April 23, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976

to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of the protection of that country; or who, not having a nationality and being outside the country of his former habitual residence as a result of such events, is unable or, owing to such fear, is unwilling to return to it.

Since Canada is not geographically located near a country from which we can expect to receive a large number of refugees, the experts, and I am referring to members of the Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate and members of Cabinet, have decided that our main role in refugee programs would consist in admitting individuals who have already been accepted as refugees in other countries. Thus, Canada is playing a fundamental part in helping first-entry countries to be more generous to people leaving their country for valid reasons. While we were expecting only a small number of people to come to Canada when we implemented our determination of refugee status system, this belief has proved to be unfounded.

Under the system provided in the Immigration Act of 1976, any person liable to be expelled from Canada can claim refugee status. This provision does not cover only those who wish to enter Canada but also those who have been residing in this country for some time as visitors or immigrants. The 1976 amendments also provided that the Refugee Status Advisory Committee would be created and make recommendations to the Minister about the validity of these applications. Under these amendments, the Minister decides whether the claims are valid, and those he turns down can then be referred to the Immigration Appeal Board.

It is at the second stage of review that the Supreme Court has ruled that a hearing is compulsory. This has allowed the claimants legal access to a standard consistent with the rights guaranteed under the Charter of Rights. However, this is not the last step in the process. Those who claim refugee status can dispute before the courts the legality of the process by which their claim was examined. They have a right to appeal under the provisions of Section 28 of the Federal Court Act, and the rulings of this court can be appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada. In the meantime, before their status is definitely established, the claimants may remain in Canada. Canada does not expel or deport those who are waiting for a ruling on their refugee status.

What has happened in fact is that the majority of claims have not been found valid by the Minister. It would be impossible to determine whether the new system allowing each claimant to be heard will produce substantially different results, even though an international survey reveals that the results of the former system were not excessive. However, it has been impossible at the administrative level to process claims rapidly, even in cases which are obviously not legitimate. The defence groups which maintain that the review process is not fair enough have encouraged the claimants to exhaust all possible legal channels. The already long delays in processing refugee claims have therefore become even longer.
As the delays have become longer, systematic attempts have been made to abuse the determination of refugee status

system. Temporary Canadian residents quickly learned that in order to remain and work in Canada, they only had to claim refugee status. It was obvious that even the weaker claims would require nearly as much time as the most complex ones. The two or three countries responsible for the greatest number of refugee status claims in Canada are in fact parliamentary democracies where the rule of law prevails and where persecution under the terms of the Convention is nearly unknown. Nearly all claims were unjustified, but they caused a complete breakdown of the review system. The waiting periods grew longer, especially since certain people understood how to exploit the system by applying for refugee status, thus avoiding being quickly expelled from Canada.

Other countries have also found themselves with an increasing number of people claiming refugee status while their country of origin was going through an economic crisis. In fact, these people wanted to leave their country of residence for purely economic reasons. Host countries, such as Germany, Sweden and Switzerland, reacted by tightening the requirements for being granted refugee status, while Canada was relaxing its own criteria.

The substantial increase in the number of people who, in the last two years, have come to Canada by requesting refugee status has put a much heavier burden on those who must rule on the legitimacy of these claims, but those who suffer the most because of this are the genuine refugees. They must often wait a long time before knowing what will happen to them, and the immigration services have no control procedure because they cannot expel from Canada those whose request has been turned down. Bona fide claimants can no longer be granted refugee status quickly.

The Advisory Committee on the Refugee Status has a huge backlog. For example, during the 18-month period from October 1983 to this day, the number of applications and appeals has gone from 9,100 to 13,500, which does not include another 600 cases always on hold for want of staff to undertake the first inquiry. The acceptance rate has dropped from 38 percent in 1981 to 33 percent recently. In addition, an increasing number of people are systematically swindling.

The Advisory Committee on Refugee Status has tried to make the system as fair and flexible as possible. The output of the Committee has been increased through the appointment of new private members and an increased administrative support. A program of personal interviews was launched in June 1983 to identify as soon as possible the true refugees. In spite of those changes, there are 3,500 cases on hold. The settlement of some matters has been sped up, but the delays continue to pile up.

The Immigration Appeal Board has known similar problems. Only the obviously deserving cases are formally heard before the Board. A year in average elapses before that hearing. In the Federal Court, the average delay for a hearing is six months at present.
April 23, 1985

Since it takes sometimes three to four years to settle certain matters, an important immigration movement has developed which the government cannot manage or control. Therefore, we must conclude that the bill does not go far enough. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) suggests that hearings be held before the Advisory Committee on Refugee Status. By doing so, there would be one more step in the process for the determination of the refugee status which already provides for a hearing. What is the purpose of this proposal? Is the present system unfair? No. Are refugees sent back home? No. The problem, Mr. Speaker, is due to increased delays and the bill of my hon. friend will in no way settle it. Therefore, I object to his proposal.

,Progressive Conservative,,Fernand Jourdenais,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c6963b2e-3dd4-4087-b65d-05d62938f08f&Language=E&Section=ALL
3525769,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.9.2.8,1985-04-23,d8c3a526-ec4a-4899-bd2e-fe277d92303e,ca.m.7652,Mrs. Lucie Pepin (Outremont):,,PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS,IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND",,"Mr. Speaker, I rise today to support Bill C-232 concerning the determination of refugee status.

As the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) pointed out, the refugee status determination process should have been reviewed long ago. Unfortunately, changes do not come easily because of the complexity of the administrative structure involved. Still, the Liberal Government had sponsored a pilot project in 1983 with a view to experimenting with a new procedure to determine refugee status. Applicants were interviewed personally by a member of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. Instead of waiting for 18 months for a decision, it often took only two months.

In my opinion, it is an excellent idea to force the Advisory Committee to hear in person the applicants for refugee status. Committee members would then be able to pass judgment more rapidly and more efficiently, and that would cut down the painful waiting period which is the lot of too many applicants. Notwithstanding what some Progessive Conservative Members may think, that would not necessarily increase the costs to be paid by Canadian taxpayers for future refugees. Efficiency does save money.

Indeed, Canadian taxpayers do not save any money when people are kept waiting for one or two years, and even four years in some cases. Refugee status applicants have a hard time earning a living and they are worried. Some of them actually become a burden to their family and friends.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-232 opens up a new vista in light of the decision of the Supreme Court to force the Immigration Appeal Board to hold personal hearings for applicants who challenge the first ruling. Is there anything more logical than hearing the personal representations of people who are concerned about their survival? The way things are now, the Committee makes a decision after considering the transcript of interviews between immigration officials and the applicant as he or she enters Canada. The parliamentary committee has heard much evidence to the effect that applicants cannot adequately express their fears and anxieties. I think that giving refugee status applicants an opportunity to present their case personally is a more compassionate way to deal with future refugees. But as I said, Mr. Speaker, humanitarian considerations aside, 1 also want to lay emphasis on the huge savings
Immigration Act, 1976
which would result from a more equitable, more effective and more humane refugee status determination process.

First of all, the costs resulting from the slowness of the bureaucratic process would be eliminated. When a case takes two or three years to move from the Refugee Status Advisory Committee to the Immigration Appeal Board, to the Federal Court, and finally to the Supreme Court, a lot of energy and hence money is wasted.

Secondly, I should like to emphasize a most interesting aspect of the 1983 pilot project. In committee, many witnesses have stated that those who are not really refugees do not like to appear personally before committee members, and that, on the contrary, the persons who are real refugees are anxious to be heard by them.

Considering that about one third of the people seeking refugee status are real refugees and that the others are caught in the process for lack of another way to come to Canada, Mr. Speaker, you will agree that such a hearing would contribute to a more equitable process for the determination of the refugee status.

There are now people who have no right to come to Canada under the Immigration Act and who are using the loopholes of the Act to do so. There is an easy scheme for those who do not fit in any of the immigrant classes. They come to a Canadian port of entry and claim refugee status as defined by the United Nations Convention. If the determination process was fair and quick, the persons wrongly seeking refugee status could be expelled in a matter of weeks. Whoever is not truly a refugee would not spend money to come to Canada and risk being deported two months later. That is a matter of common sense, is it not?

Mr. Speaker, the people who are not really refugees know that it can take as much as five years for their case to move from the first level of decision making to the last. They find it worthwhile to borrow money and take the complicated steps required in order to find a haven for five years.

Those are facts which are common knowledge abroad among the people living in communities with a large number of potential emigrants. They are also common knowledge in Canada among the ethnic groups where people want to help a distant relative or friend to come to Canada. This works against real refugees who need immediate assistance and whose lives may be in danger in their countries of origin, and it works also against Canadian taxpayers.

It would be easy indeed to blame the current problems on the Liberal Party. But it is not so simple. I mentioned earlier a pilot project introduced by the Liberal government in 1983. The responsibilities of those in power cannot be underestimated or excused on another political group. Any government can always act to solve the problems Canadians have to face.

It can be said that the Conservative government has acted quickly to change a number of administrative practices in the area of immigration. Last fall, the Minister ordered immigration officers not to provide prospective immigrants, including refugees, with any legal aid during the hearings they have with
April 23, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976

them. As 1 indicated earlier, the Advisory Committee on refugee status decides whether the applicant will be admitted or not on the basis of these interviews. Now, these interviews are very intimidating for those people who do not know our laws or customs and who know that a wrong answer can send them right back to their country to live in difficult conditions.

Another example of the will of the Conservative Party to change our immigration policy is the over emphasis put on the entrepreneurs' program. Conservative members of the Parliamentary Committee are more concerned with the need to give a first-rate treatment to investors immigrants than with the need to deal with social problems resulting from the present situation.

Whereas Conservative members of the Committee want to increase the number of immigrants from 85,000 this year to 200,000 in 1986, they are not as willing to grant them the minimum services for an adequate integration.

We know that the lack of services which I would call essential, is sometimes rather serious. The Conservative Party thinks it will save money by cutting into services to immigrants whereas the social effects resulting from this lack of services are more costly than those services themselves.

The refusal to provide a language training course to all those who need it will eventually lead to immigrants being combined in ghettos and in low-paid and tedious jobs. If, later on, immigrants have to apply for unemploymnt or welfare benefits, that will foster racism. People will say that they are taking advantage of the work of Canadians.

Now, Mr. Speaker, many people who have to work with immigrants will tell you that those people are eager to work, to earn their living and support their families and to contribute to the economic development of Canada. However, in order for them to do so, they must have available to them the tools that will enable them to get integrated in a normal way into the Canadian society. They must have available to them services paid for by Canadians who will get largely repaid for them. This is what is important to understand when speaking of services provided to immigrants.

Bill C-232 giving claimants to refugee status the right to be heard in person by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee is a step toward a process of determination of the refugee status more equitable for everybody; perhaps in this way we will see an end to the many and unspeakable abuses of which the prospective refugees are the victims.

Those abuses are terrible, Mr. Speaker, and are not a great credit to Canada. Some journalists from The Globe and Mail asked a few prospective immigrants to go to some consultants or lawyers specialized in immigration matters. Those prospective immigrants had fictitious backgrounds totally unacceptable under the Immigration Act. Yet those people were told by almost every consultant and lawyer consulted that they could get admitted for a fee of $500 in one case, $1,500 in another case and $4,000 in a third case. It would therefore be necessary to regulate the immigration consultants since those consultants deal with those who are totally unaware of the

Canadian laws and standards. As for lawyers specialized in immigration matters, the Bar takes upon itself to penalize them. It remains however that few immigrants will have the courage to question the fees or the quality of services offered by the lawyers because this requires knowledge in the field.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe Bill C-232 is a step in the right direction. I am sure that a more equitable process of determination of the refugee status will allow savings for Canadian taxpayers, and will be more humanitarian for prospective immigrants.

This will be a more efficient way for us to fulfill our international duty of welcoming refugees. Finally, since the Supreme Court recently ruled in a similar way regarding the Immigration Appeal Board, the process of determination of the refugee status will also be more logical.

,Liberal,,Lucie Pépin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d8c3a526-ec4a-4899-bd2e-fe277d92303e&Language=E&Section=ALL
3525770,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.9.2.9,1985-04-23,9f07b251-28cf-4c2a-9279-90ee2a01d2c8,ca.m.6664,Mr. John Oostrom (Willowdale):,,PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS,IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND",,"Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to participate in the debate on Bill C-232 on the subject of refugees, introduced by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).

The Hon. Member for Spadina called this Government thick-headed and accused it of stonewalling on various issues. 1 would rather commend it and say that Canada's efforts in formulating and administering the refugee policy is one 1 believe we can look at with pride. After all, Canada has accommodated more refugees per capita than virtually any other country in the world. We have only to remind the House of the 50,000 Vietnamese refugees we took in. In addition to those from Vietnam, people came from Iran, South America and many other countries, especially eastern Europe.

Canadians have shown the capacity to care, that often neglected quality of reaching out to those who are suffering persecution for reasons of race, religion or politics, of giving comfort to the homeless and the stateless. We have also shown a concern to ensure that our institutions and our administrative practices reflect those humanitarian ideals that we have set for ourselves.

What we are concerned with here today is the maintenance of a realistic balance. The hard truth is that we must weigh our humanitarian instincts and goals against the obligation that every sovereign state has of maintaining the integrity of its borders. In other words, our international commitment to refugees must be fulfilled in tandem with immigration control factors and the protection of the interests of Canada.

Unlike other countries, Canada has not until recently faced the phenomenon of large numbers of people claiming refugee status suddenly appearing at our doorsteps. In the past, geography has acted as a buffer, if you will, providing a degree of isolation from turbulence in other lands that gave rise to large numbers of refugees. In many respects, this is a shrinking world. The movement of people either as tourists or immigrants has increased. Canada welcomes many visitors and newcomers each year to her shores. In fact, we have benefited
April 23, 1985
from the dramatic increase of world travel because of the tourist trade. By the same token, we are no longer isolated from other countries where strife and civil unrest are not uncommon.

According to reliable estimates, there are some 70 million to 80 million people in the world today who have been permanently displaced from their homes. They move because of war, revolution, poverty, or simply in the hope of creating a better future for themselves and their children. Some of these people are refugees, others are not. The challenge is to distinguish between the two in a way that is fair and practical.

A procedure was established after we signed the Geneva Convention in 1969 whereby an individual could claim recognition as a convention refugee, either upon arriving in Canada or after admission to Canada if that person faced removal from Canada. Later, in 1978, the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, separate from the established program on immigration in the Immigration Department, was set up for the sole purpose of advising the Minister on refugee claims. The Minister was given the power to appoint committee members, but it was given little in the way of additional guidelines.

The creation of the advisory committee was a bold step in the evolution of a refugee policy, but there was some criticism. Some critics felt that the committee's recommendations were too harsh or arbitrary, that the United Nation's definition of a refugee was unduly restrictive and that the system did not provide adequate guarantees or fairness to all claimants.

in February of 1982, the Government acted to move the entire system in the direction of increased fairness and openness. The new reforms clearly separated the refugee determination process from immigration procedures to ensure that refugee cases are assessed on the basis of human rights considerations alone. Earlier this month, the Supreme Court concluded that the system designed in the late 1970s does not meet the standard of justice required under the Canadian Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, and has indicated that all claimants must be heard orally by the Immigration Appeal Board.

While our refugee determination system has been undergoing a process of reform and liberalization, more and more of the world's people have become refugees as a result of war, persecution and minority-majority conflict. Inevitably, the people displaced by these factors look toward the industrialized nations for help. The channel of last resort is that provided by the refugee asylum structures in developed countries like Canada. Even though these channels do not provide guarantees of long-term help for these people, these structures provide access to work and social benefits, at least on a temporary basis.

As more people use these systems, the greater the backlog and the longer the delays, even for those whose claims on the refugee determination system are tenuous at best. Thus the potential for abuse is great indeed. Since 1980, we have witnessed a manifold increase in the number of refugee ciaim-
Immigration Act, 1976
ants. This places an enormous strain on our resettlement resources.

Recent refugee claimant arrivals have averaged about 600 a month. About 13,500 cases are now under review, as the Hon. Member for Spadina said earlier, and more are under judicial appeal. Yet, only about one-third of those who claim refugee status have their claims upheld. Many of the claimants have been using the refugee system to get around our immigration laws. Not only is this unfair to those who are legitimately following the procedures, but it jeopardizes the entire immigration system.

I believe we would be faced with a serious dilemma if we were to endorse the proposed Bill. After all, claimants already have a right to an oral hearing at the Immigration Appeal Board. I doubt their protections will be enhanced by two oral hearings. We would, as I have stated earlier, appear to be improving the determination process, while in fact we would be undermining the claims process through further delay. By lengthening the period of time that individuals would be able to remain in Canada, more people will be drawn into the process, because being in it gives them access to working in Canada, living here, and in some cases drawing social benefits normally reserved for permanent residents.

Our Immigration Act recognizes in law our humanitarian concerns, and through the refugee determination system that exists today we are able to ensure that no one is sent from this country until he or she has received a full assessment of his or her refugee claim. One of the lawyers dealing with these cases, Patricia Ann Ritter, referred to me the case of Mr. Simon Bancroft Hall. His detention was reviewed on a weekly basis, pursuant to statute, and on April 9, the first working day for the commission after the Supreme Court of Canada decision, at a review of Mr. Hall's detention, the senior immigration officer submitted that it was the position that in light of the decision Mr. Hall would be heard as he had been denied an oral hearing previously. Something is being done.

This is not to say that the system is without problems, but to deal with these problems on a piecemeal basis is not really the answer. Therefore, we on this side of the House can only conclude that the Bill would do nothing to enhance the fairness and openness of the refugee determination system.

,Progressive Conservative,,John Martin Oostrom,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9f07b251-28cf-4c2a-9279-90ee2a01d2c8&Language=E&Section=ALL
3525771,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.9.2.10,1985-04-23,4354b438-9a7b-4fa7-ad25-e6847c4caf60,ca.m.1856,Mr. Gordon Taylor (Bow River):,,PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS,IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND",,"Mr. Speaker, after the very splendid address we just heard, I would like to enlarge on one or two points.

I believe our immigration system must be very fair. It has to be fair to Canadians who are living here now, and many Canadians who are jobless feel that the immigration laws are too lax. However, the laws must be fair to those in other countries who are trying to come to this country and who are doing so legally. I think we must emphasize that particular point.

There is a growing feeling in Canada that too many people are coming to our nation. I do not think anyone objects to people coming to our country because of terrible conditions in their own lands, but those who come here in a purposely illegal
April 23, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
fashion should not be considered. I cannot follow the fact that some of them are waiting here for six and eight years.

One of my constituents contacted me when one of his relatives came to Canada from Yugoslavia. This man had applied twice to come to Canada and had been rejected. However, he came anyway. He got on a plane and simply came to Canada irrespective of the law. 1 do not think that is fair to those who make applications and wait for approval in their own countries. This man had a hearing in Toronto within two weeks of his arrival. My constituent contacted me and said that the man was here. He told me how he got here. I said I would get the hearing set as quickly as possible. I contacted officials and the hearing was held within two weeks. That man was sent back to his country. He claimed that he could not go back because he would be killed. That was nonsense and his relatives told us that. We were told that that was simply an excuse to leave his own country. Later on we found out that he wanted to leave his wife and three kids. That is like a Canadian who gets married in Alberta, gets divorced and leaves his wife on welfare rather than pay maintenance orders. These Canadians end up in Prince Edward Island, or any other province, with a common-law wife and more youngsters, following which he heads for British Columbia in order to avoid another maintenance order. That kind of person is no good to any country.

I believe we have to be absolutely fair to those wonderful citizens of other countries who want to enter Canada, and want to do so legally. I have no sympathy for those who come here illegally. I do not think they should be kept here for six, seven or eight years. If they come to Canada illegally they should be sent back immediately. They should not be kept here month after month when they have no right to be here at all. If an immigrant enters Canada and is classified as a refugee, he should not have special privileges over those who are entering Canada legally from China, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, Japan, Korea or any other country. He should not have special privileges simply because he did something under the table. Let us give those who want to come to Canada legally the first opportunities. Let us not cry crocodile tears for those who come here illegally. Let us not try to keep them in the country month after month.

An Hon. Member mentioned that people were paying $1,500 to come here. The Hon. Member should let us have the names of those people, because I am sure the Minister would prosecute them. We do not want people to buy their way into Canada. We want them to come in legally. Those who come in legally are the kind of people who will make good citizens.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Edward Taylor,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4354b438-9a7b-4fa7-ad25-e6847c4caf60&Language=E&Section=ALL

3525775,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.2.1,1985-04-23,19484d4b-ea72-419e-8a5f-7077c4906de5,ca.m.1156,Mr. Alan Redway (York East):,,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,PORNOGRAPHY-FRASER COMMISSION REPORT,,Mr. Speaker, on March 22 1 asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) when we could expect to have the Fraser Committee Report dealing with pornography, and when we would be in a position to start to deal with that subject and tighten up the laws, rules and regulations of this country with respect to pornography. The Minister at that time advised me that the report was coming shortly. I am pleased to say that by some interesting coincidence the report of many, many pages dealing with the subject of pornography was released today. I know that the people of this country are very pleased that it is out so that we can start to deal with this subject.

Pornography is something which I suppose has been around as long as history itself. The fact that it has been around, however, does not deter from the fact that at this time it poses a very serious problem in this country. In recent years we have seen a great increase in the volume of pornorgraphy over that of a few years ago. Pornography is also of a much more explicit and violent variety. In fact, I venture to say that most of the things which we see on our television screens, in print and in theatres today are things which would not have been tolerated just a few years ago.

Pornography now is seen and observed by the public not only in books, the theatre and on the movie screens, but of course daily on television and also now on video casettes. Everyone is concerned about this subject but we have not been able to come to grips with it. There are a variety of reasons for that, but it is basically that there is a great difference of opinion and variance in attitude towards the entire subject of pornography. Many people share my view and my concern that not only is it something which offends taste but it is also something which is inherently harmful to society and does have the potential for breeding violence against other people, either of a sexual or otherwise criminal nature.

There is a concern as well on the part of many of us that there is a softening up process going on. We are being bombarded constantly with this sort of material and that has a tendency to soften everyone to the whole concept. Over time, people start to feel that there is nothing wrong with this sort of material. On the other hand, there are many people in the country, Mr. Speaker, who feel that to restrict and limit pornography is in fact some sort of infringement on basic human rights and an infringement on freedom of speech. It is because of that sort of feeling that we have this great conflict and are unable to come to grips with the whole subject.
April 23, 1985

I firmly believe, however, that even those who feel there is a restriction on freedom of speech in doing something to restrict pornography believe as well as the rest of us that child pornography is a real problem and of concern, is something which should be restricted and dealt with. I am pleased to see that the Fraser Commission Report does deal with the very subject of child pornography. It suggests that it should be an offence when it involves those under the age of 18. That deals very clearly with the concern that while adults perhaps can consent and understand what all of this is about, children cannot. Clearly it should be an offence and I am very pleased to see that covered in the Fraser Report. I would hope that the Government will deal quickly with that aspect of the report.

The other aspect, of course, is that which deals with pornography generally and the question of whether there should be some other restrictions on pornography, apart from child pornography. The Fraser Committee has again outlined recommendations dealing with that.

The Fraser Committee is not the first forum which has made some recommendations regarding this kind of pornography. I understand this Flouse dealt with the subject in a previous Bill. There have been recommendations from feminist groups and from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Many of their concerns focus on two points. First of all, the question of whether pornography should be defined according to a public standard or whether there should be some objective test to deal with pornography, and secondly, whether it is only sexual acts which should be considered as pornography, or that violence should be considered separately. The Fraser Committee has recommended that there should be two separate offenses there, and also that we have an objective test.

It remains to be seen how quickly the Government will act on this matter, but I hope that the consultations have now come to an end. We have studied this subject long enough, and I hope the Government will now act very quickly. I am looking forward to hearing from the Parliamentary Secretary on the Government's response, and how soon it will act.

,Progressive Conservative,,Alan Redway,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=19484d4b-ea72-419e-8a5f-7077c4906de5&Language=E&Section=ALL
3525776,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.2.2,1985-04-23,761a9263-10e4-4b7c-848d-e7ba3a1f500e,ca.m.2746,Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):,Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,PORNOGRAPHY-FRASER COMMISSION REPORT,,Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's concern about this very serious problem. As he said, the report of the Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution was tabled by the Minister today. The Committee benefited from the submissions and briefs which were received in the public hearings and from research done by the Department of Justice. There are upwards of 100 recommendations contained in the report which will require consideration by the Government.

The Government especially wants to consult with the provincial Attorneys General in order to deal with the people who are on the, shall we say, practice end of any laws we pass-the people who have to prosecute. Naturally we want to see that the laws suggested in this House by this Government are capable of being put into practice at the working level by the
Adjournment Debate
people who handle them. In addition, there will be public interest groups which will want to be heard on the direction these amendments should take.

I can tell the Hon. Member that the Minister is especially concerned about the dramatic increase in sexually explicit material which has become more widespread and more readily available throughout Canada. I can assure him that the Minister will carefully consider the Fraser Committee's recommendations before proceeding to draft and introduce legislative proposals in respect of pornography and prostitution, and that such proposals will not be introduced prior to consultation with the Attorneys General. The legislation that we hope will result from this process will be developed only after careful study and consideration, and we welcome the Hon. Member's participation in that process just as we welcome that of any Member of Parliament.

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Grinslade Lewis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=761a9263-10e4-4b7c-848d-e7ba3a1f500e&Language=E&Section=ALL

3525778,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.3.1,1985-04-23,608d24d3-2228-4a1c-9f28-30630d28a48f,ca.m.6620,Miss Aideen Nicholson (Trinity):,,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,TRUST COMPANIES-WESTERN CAPITAL TRUST. (B) MINISTER'S STATEMENT,,Mr. Speaker, on April 3 I raised with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) the matter of a discrepancy between an event occuring on March 29 and a statement made by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) in the House on the same day. The event was the failure of Western Capital Trust in British Columbia barely one week after the Government announced its plan to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank.
On March 29, during the debate on the Government's Bill to bail out that bank, the Minister described that situation as an isolated incident.
The Minister said:
There are no other financial institutions in the country at the moment that arc appearing to be insolvent in any way.

On April 3 I asked why the Minister of State for Finance would have said that to the House when she surely must have known that Western Capital Trust was in serious difficulty and was closing its doors as she spoke. The Minister of Finance replied that the remark of the Minister of State for Finance arose from her hope of success in the company's merger negotiations and that departmental officials had been meeting with Western Capital Trust over the winter on this matter.

That response makes no sense at all. The Minister of State for Finance said that no institution other than the Canadian Commercial Bank was in difficulty on the very day that Western Capital Trust announced that it was obliged to wind up its operations. Naturally, I take it for granted that the Minister would not intentionally mislead the House. The only remaining explanation is that she did not know what was going on. Why did she not know? Did her officials fail to brief her? Did the Minister of Finance fail to inform her?
April 23, 1985
Adjournment Debate
Let us look at the chronology again so that this will be quite clear. On February 12 the Minister of State for Finance, responding to a question about another trust company, said:
I would like to reassure the House with respect to other western trust companies, that I'm not aware of any which are on the brink of collapse.

On March 29 the Minister also said that no institution, other than the Canadian Commercial Bank, was in any difficulty. On March 29 Western Capital Trust closed its doors. On April 2 the Minister of State for Finance then said that officials in the Department of Finance had met continually over the winter months with officials from Western Capital Trust. On April 3 the Minister of Finance said:

Mr. Speaker, for some months now the Government has been working with Western Capital Trust to try to assist it in merging with another, stronger trust company. At the time the Minister made that statement it was expected that those merger negotiations would be completed successfully. That is the basis for her comments.
Again, that simply does not make sense since the company in question, Western Capital Trust, was closing its doors even as the Minister spoke.

The issue of confidence in our financial institution is, of course, very important. The whole system depends on confidence. It is the cornerstone of our financial system. Members of the Opposition who ask questions in the House do not do so out of a desire to undermine confidence in the system. In this case, all the questions that I asked came long after the events had been made public. When Ministers make statements which appear to be contradicted by fact, and do not explain the discrepancy, it does not inspire confidence. I hope that, given the opportunity now, the Government will give the House a clear statement.

,Liberal,,Aideen Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=608d24d3-2228-4a1c-9f28-30630d28a48f&Language=E&Section=ALL
3525779,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.3.2,1985-04-23,761a9263-10e4-4b7c-848d-e7ba3a1f500e,ca.m.2746,Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):,Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,TRUST COMPANIES-WESTERN CAPITAL TRUST. (B) MINISTER'S STATEMENT,,Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to elaborate on the situation for the benefit of the Member, who obviously has put a lot of thought into her comments.

Western Capital Trust had been monitored by officials of the department of Insurance for some time. In that regard, the examiners of the Department of Insurance, following an inspection of the books and records of the company in late 1984, concluded that the company had some $3 million worth of capital, but that additional capital was required to fully comply with the borrowing provisions of the Trust Companies Act. The company's annual financial statement was filed with the Department on February 28, 1985, indicating that the company had $3 million of capital at December 31, 1984. In an accompanying letter the company's auditors indicated that the financial position of the company was fairly presented in the annual statement.

During 1984, several different plans had been put forward to enable the company to fully comply with the borrowing provisions of the Trust Companies Act. The company sold large blocks of mortgages for cash to reduce borrowing, and it tried to arrange for private placement of preference shares. But none of these courses of action were successful so a formal
report on the company's overborrowed situation was submitted by the Superintendent to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall).

That report recommended that limitations be placed on the company's licence so as to reduce its borrowings and thereby bring the company into compliance with the Act. The President of the company chose to revive negotiations to merge Western Capital Trust Company and another corporation. 3525781,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.4.1,1985-04-23,c561ac11-18ab-4c6c-8b7b-86b2e5484dfd,ca.m.4172,Ms. Margaret Mitchell (Vancouver East):,,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,CHARTER OF RIGHTS-WOMEN'S EQUALITY-ABELLA REPORT. (B) AFFIRMATIVE ACTION,,Mr. Speaker, on February 1, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) to take positive action on the question of equality. Specifically, I asked him to act on the Abella Commission recommendations to legislate mandatory affirmative action and contract compliance before April 17, when the Charter of Rights would come into force. We have now received the Government report on employment equity which was tabled by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss Macdonald) a number of weeks ago.

Critics from my Party felt that the Government proposals were weak. We expressed our concern that there was no enforcement mechanism for contract compliance and companies which have contracts with the Government were left to establish their own targets for employment equity. As with the Liberals before, Tories seem to be reluctant to enforce mandatory affirmative action.

I also asked that funding for the Human Rights Commission be increased so that adequate staff may be hired to deal with the many additional complaints which will result from the Government's equity program. For several years we have had federal legislation which requires equal pay for work of equal
April 23, 1985

value so that women will be paid at the same rate as men in similar job responsibilities. Despite this legislation, there has not been systematic change even within areas of federal jurisdiction. 1 have urged the Government to enforce equal value pay in every department and Crown corporation so that women will no longer have to appeal individually on a case by case basis to the Human Rights Commission.

On April 17 we celebrated the Charter of Rights and the coming into being of the equality clause. Having equality rights on paper, however, does not mean that people will be treated equally. Unfortunately, the Conservative Government delayed changes to legislation, and also to regulations which are clearly discriminatory and do not conform to the Charter. For example, the discrimination under the Unemployment Insurance Act is evident because it unfairly restricts benefits for unemployed women on maternity leave. They are eligible for fewer benefits because they happen to be pregnant. Another example concerns maternity leave in the military. We support the position of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women on this very important issue.

Another example of unfairness is the fact that while the Government has given lip-service to equality compliance in Crown corporations, Air Canada is establishing a very negative precedent by trying to bargain away women's rights to full-time jobs that are decently paid.

The Government by its inaction now has forced women to fight legal and very expensive battles to achieve their rights under the New Charter of Rights. A legal assistance fund is necessary to undertake test cases before the courts. Such a fund should be independent of government and political bias. I asked the Minister of Justice recently to celebrate equality on April 17 by generously contributing to the legal education assistance fund which has been established as an endowment for legal challenges by women related to equality under the Charter. Once again the Minister of Justice refused to act. This Government's inaction was a disappointment on this memorable and historic day.

3525782,ca.proc.d.1985-04-23.10.4.2,1985-04-23,d590d6af-797b-4896-aa69-6365eb37655e,ca.m.9482,Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration,PROCEEDINGS ON ADJOURNMENT MOTION,CHARTER OF RIGHTS-WOMEN'S EQUALITY-ABELLA REPORT. (B) AFFIRMATIVE ACTION,,Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for closely following the issue of equality in employment, which became even more important with the proclamation, on April 17 last, of the relevant provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The Hon. Member knows, since she has just mentioned that fact, that women and minorities are the people who celebrated last week the historical proclamation of the provisions on equality which our Government acted to amend in the context of the debate on equality in employment.
Adjournment Debate

The Hon. Member will also remember that on March 8, in this House, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced the implementation of measures for employment equity, the very words used by Judge Abella which singularly expresses the goals we are pursuing in order that women, natives, handicapped people and visible minorities may prove their worth in the workplace.

It was announced then, Mr. Speaker, that following study, debate and consultation, we would be introducing measures of unprecedented scope, the effects of which will be as far-reaching as the Hon. Member and myself might wish them to be.

In short, our action with respect to employment equity will consist of the adoption, by the federal Government, of decisive measures in employment sectors coming under its control and its jurisdiction. In the process, Mr. Speaker, we are encouraging provincial Governments and municipalities in implementing positive action programs.

Before the end of this session, Mr. Speaker, we will table in this House a legislation that will seek to make it mandatory for companies subject to federal regulations and having less than one hundred employees to take action to achieve employment equity and report each year to this House on their efforts in that area. Such legislation is presently in preparation and, as announced by the Hon. Minister on March 8 last, we are consulting with the representatives of the industry, the unions and the target groups on the way to present those reports. Furthermore, we are formulating directives in this regard.

We have also asked Crown corporations to implement equity measures in the area of employment, and to take the steps needed to be able to present to Parliament annual reports on their performance through the ministers responsible for those corporations.

Mr. Speaker, we are developing a program of contracts related to the implementation of equity measures in the area of employment. Under this program, businesses which have contracts exceeding $200,000 and have at least 100 employees will also have to implement equity measures in the area of employment, and we will control their implementation.
In all those areas, our action is based to a large extent on the conclusions and recommendations of the Abella report.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the Hon. Member, like women and minorities all over the country, will realize that we are taking strong and responsible steps to promote equity in the area of employment, and we hope we can count on her support when the legislation is tabled in this House.
April 23, 1985
Adjournment Debate
